action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'pin', 'unpin'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

43	### A1. What a number on a tile means — and the engine that works it out

Three defects follow, all on the Hormuz map today: *This happened* on Brent does not move what caused it; supposing the insurance premium or OPEC+ restraint moves Brent and moves **neither trade at all**; and a claim nobody believes can wipe out your own *Suppose*.
46	
47	**Proposed:** the number becomes *the chance it happens by its deadline*. Whether each claim happens is solved exactly; when it happens is sampled forward. The arrows keep their lag, shape and half-life. Measured on small adversarial maps: right to four decimal places for *Suppose*. **Not yet right for *This happened*** — the first design was off by up to .12 there, so the stack opens with a one-session spike (three candidates, a kill criterion) before any product code.

49	*On screen:* every number on the Hormuz map changes once, in one reviewable diff. Supposing OPEC+ restraint finally moves the Brent trade.

52	- **Recommended: yes, opening with the spike.** It is the cheapest way found to honour both of your answers — exact, and the time model kept. `review2`'s own version of "exact" measured at 0.7–8 seconds a range on a 20-claim map; this one at half a millisecond.
53	- Alternative: repair today's engine in place. Costed: it breaks the range or the locality proof, and leaves the third defect. Not recommended.
54	- Alternative: do nothing and ship the thesis on today's numbers. The card would then rest on trades that are deaf to half their causes.

56	### A2. `sustain`: events and states, or events only? — *you must pick; "leave it" is not available*

## The questions as they were put

**Status when written: WAITING ON KENT. Nothing marked here was built until he answered.** Each question is in plain words, with the Hormuz example, what changes on screen and in code, and the recommended option first. The reasoning is in `design-after-midpoint-review.md`; the evidence in `analysis/`. When he answers, record his words here, dated, and fold them into `PLAN.md` the same day.

**Already his, and not re-asked** — his four answers to `review2` on 2026-09-21: *an exact core with a sampler on top · keep the time model and make it sound · land what is open, then finance before more generation · revisit generation.* And today: *only Hormuz is recorded until he explicitly approves more*; *the spec stays a first-class book — shorten it where warranted, not as a maxim.*

**In force from earlier rounds** (K1–K11, G1–G13, S1–S8) unless a row below says it would be superseded.

---

## A. Needed before stack 05 can start

### A1. What a number on a tile means — and the engine that works it out

**Today:** a claim's number is a snapshot read on its deadline. Three defects follow, all on the Hormuz map today: *This happened* on Brent does not move what caused it; supposing the insurance premium or OPEC+ restraint moves Brent and moves **neither trade at all**; and a claim nobody believes can wipe out your own *Suppose*.

**Proposed:** the number becomes *the chance it happens by its deadline*. Whether each claim happens is solved exactly; when it happens is sampled forward. The arrows keep their lag, shape and half-life. Measured on small adversarial maps: right to four decimal places for *Suppose*. **Not yet right for *This happened*** — the first design was off by up to .12 there, so the stack opens with a one-session spike (three candidates, a kill criterion) before any product code.

*On screen:* every number on the Hormuz map changes once, in one reviewable diff. Supposing OPEC+ restraint finally moves the Brent trade.
*In code:* `propagation.py` and much of `diff.py` rewritten behind a flag, then one flip. Branches, the validator, locality and the wire shapes stay. **8–12 sessions for the stack.**

- **Recommended: yes, opening with the spike.** It is the cheapest way found to honour both of your answers — exact, and the time model kept. `review2`'s own version of "exact" measured at 0.7–8 seconds a range on a 20-claim map; this one at half a millisecond.
- Alternative: repair today's engine in place. Costed: it breaks the range or the locality proof, and leaves the third defect. Not recommended.
- Alternative: do nothing and ship the thesis on today's numbers. The card would then rest on trades that are deaf to half their causes.

### A2. `sustain`: events and states, or events only? — *you must pick; "leave it" is not available*

Once something that happened can never un-happen, a `sustain` arrow and a `trigger` arrow become **identical** (measured: six decimal places). Record 0005 called that pair the best idea in the brainstorm, and you asked to keep it. It survives only in one of these forms:

- **(i) Events and states — recommended.** *The strait reopens* is an event: once it happened, it happened. *The strait stays open to commercial transit through 1 November* is a state: it can stop holding. A `sustain` arrow may only leave a state. **Automatic retraction is deleted** — so *"Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck"* finally leaves both events standing, and the strike lowers the state everything downstream depends on. *On screen:* the strike branch reads *opened (supposed) · stays open through 1 Nov: .08 · Brent below $68: .30* instead of *opened: withdrawn*; the retraction badge and two day-states go. *In code:* mostly deletion on the canvas; a state needs an on-time and an off-time in the engine; the model must say which kind each claim is, so it rides the one shape freeze. **Reverses record 0014, decision A — yours.** About 3 sessions more than (ii).
- **(ii) Events only; a sustained push is two arrows** — one from the event that starts it, an inhibitor from the event that ends it. Same arithmetic, one validity rule, one prompt sentence, no new field. `mode` and the word *sustain* leave the vocabulary. Cheapest sound option.
- Either way the third defect dies, because both delete retraction-by-calendar.

### A3. The path product → the shift, the joint, and the weakest arrow

INV-8 and FR-11 (P0) require *"the multiplied-out likelihood of the path."* Both reviews and three analysts: multiplying along a route is not the chance of anything when claims share a cause (if Y always equals X and both are .5, the product says .25; the truth is .5).

- **Recommended: replace it.** The Verify door says instead: *"Reopening moves the Brent claim by 32 points, from .24 to .56. Every step on the best-backed route goes right in 19% of worlds. The arrow carrying most of that shift is 'reopening → shipping recovers'; delete it and 71% of the effect goes."* (Illustrative numbers — the real ones come from the engine.) Three real quantities, one or two extra solves each. INV-8 becomes *"chains are worked out, not multiplied."* The item that would have moved the product into `domain/` is already dropped.
- Alternative: keep it, labelled as what it is. It stays a number that is not a probability, on the screen that answers the brief's first use case.

### A4. The spread changes the scripted strike — look, then say yes or overturn

With the provenance spread on (your rule, record 0014), the strike branch shows **two ranked rows instead of three**. Brent (B) and *talks resume* (N1) read `unchanged`. N1 makes the biggest move on the map, `.28 → .38`, but its only arrow is the map's one bare assertion, so only 88 versions in 100 agree which way — under your 90% bar. The tile now says why: *versions disagree*.

- **Recommended: accept it, and show a disagreeing row greyed on the list with its reason rather than dropping it.** It is the product telling the truth about an arrow nobody can back. You will see it at M4; all four spec passages that describe it are in one commit (`f9d86ce`) so it is easy to overturn.
- Alternative: give the N1 arrow a source in the fixture, which makes it `documented` and narrow. Honest only if a source exists.

---

## B. Needed before the one paid re-recording (stack 05's last step)

### B1. Pay once — confirm the order

The payoff `kind` fix is written and clean, but it changes what we ask the model, which makes `hormuz.jsonl` stale (~$4, ~40 min to re-make). The engine work and the evidence work will change what we ask **again**.

- **Recommended: land today's recording as it is (it is valid against `main`); hold the `kind` fix; batch every such change into one freeze *after* the engine has proven what it needs to be told; record once** (~$5, ~45 min, in the background). The defect is latent — the model filled the field in all eleven trades.
- Alternative: land the fix now and record twice (~$10, ~90 min).

### B2. One number per arrow, in words a trader can argue with

Today the model writes an abstract `strength`, and the description we send it says *"+1 triples the odds"* — a number **we** invented, inside a prompt. Proposed: the claim's own number is asked as *the chance it happens by its deadline if none of the causes on this map happens*; each arrow as *the chance if this cause happens at the start of the window and no other cause does.* Our code derives the weight.

*On screen:* the Inspector stops saying *strength 2.2* and says *"war-risk premiums falling takes Brent below $68 from 24% to 56%."*
- **Recommended: yes.** About 0.7 session, inside the freeze.
- Alternative: keep `strength`, only bound it. Half a session cheaper; keeps our anchor.

### B3. Twenty-five searches a claim (G7): keep, narrow, or drop

Measured on your recording: 93 searches bought **five** base rates across eighteen claims, and three of the five are *0 of 2*, *2 of 3*, *1 of 1*. A call that searches takes 3–4× as long; this is where most of the 36 minutes went.

- **Recommended: narrow it** — no search on the first call (a first tile in ~7 s, measured), none on a price threshold, and a count under five is dropped rather than printed. Saves about a third of the clock.
- Alternative: keep G7 as it is.

### B4. A source says what it is for

Today a source is a URL the search returned. Proposed: the model also gives **the sentence on that page that carries the weight** and **what it supports** (mechanism · magnitude · timing · resolution · instrument); the Inspector shows quote, role, link. The showcase's trade-critical sources are checked by hand once. (`review2`'s automatic check cannot be built — the search tool returns encrypted text.)
- **Recommended: yes**, inside the freeze.

### B5. The other three recordings — your instruction stands; this is the case for lifting it later

The brief names four example inputs and FR-3 (P0) puts all four on the launchpad. Your concern was time. Recorded **once, after the freeze, three at once in the background**, it is about **45 minutes of wall clock and ~$15**, not two-plus hours back to back, and it blocks nothing while it runs.
- **Recommended: approve it for that moment, not before.** Until you do, only Hormuz is recorded and the definition of done shows that box unticked, with the reason.

---

## C. Needed before stack 06

### C1. The stop-loss is a price you own; what we derive is a watchlist

`spec/thesis/` says the stop-loss *"is derived, not guessed"*, and PRD anti-pattern 11 says *"do not type the stop-loss by hand."* On your own fixture the derivation yields nothing usable: the only claim that resolves before the Brent trade is the thing the thesis is betting on.

*On screen, three sections where there was one:* **What takes you out** — computed: the events over-represented in the worlds where your stop is hit first (the brief's most distinctive sentence, answered by arithmetic). **What to watch** — computed: the adverse flip that hurts most, resolves earlier, and can be observed. **Your exit** — stop, target, horizon: you type them.
- **Recommended: yes.** Amends INV-14, FR-22, FR-23, FR-24; reverses anti-pattern 11. Near-zero code for the renaming; the lift query is ~40 lines.
- Alternative: keep the wording — and a claim no risk quant would let stand.

### C2. Does the Brent trade name a real Polymarket contract?

The fixture's contract is an honest stand-in. The demo's climax is *"the model says .46, the venue says .48."* Nobody has looked at the venue.
- **Recommended: half an hour by hand on Polymarket; if a live Brent or oil contract exists, rewrite the ending to name it exactly and record its quote.** If none exists, the card says *"no contract quotes this claim — edge not calculable"* and prints a break-even, which is honest and still useful.

### C3. Sessions in a SQLite file (FR-31, P0) — build, shrink, or cut?

It is scheduled nowhere and cut nowhere. Today a generated map lives in the server's memory and is gone on restart.
- **Recommended: shrink it to the format you already have.** A kept run is already written to disk as the same line-by-line file a recording is; serve a finished generation back from that file by its id. One format, one loader, no database, no migration. Amend FR-31 to say so. About one session.
- Alternative: cut it for version one, with a line in the *what version one does not build* record.
- Alternative: build SQLite as written. 2–3 sessions for something the walk never exercises.

---

## D. Process — any time

### D1. Stacks two deep (amends record 0009 — yours)
Four-deep stacks cost this stack a three-case rebase recipe, a file-ownership table and four days with `main` static. **Recommended:** a docs bottom and one code pull request on it, otherwise straight onto `main`. Commit convention, branch names, the three headings, squash-merge, always green: unchanged.

### D2. One owning place for the worked example's numbers
About 90 engine-computed numbers are quoted across 13 committed files, and the README's `curl` example prints 16 digits a reader will not get. **Recommended:** `make numbers` writes one committed file; the build fails when it is stale (the pattern `types-fresh` already uses); chapters quote and link. The strict version — no computed number in any document — would delete about a hundred passages that teach.

### D3. Local cuts to the spec
None is a freeze; each rides in the pull request that touches the chapter. The largest: **one line of the chapter template** asks for *"the pydantic models verbatim"* — those sections run to about 35 000 words and are 50–79% identical to the code. **Recommended:** a *Data model* section gives the shape and its reasons, and names the module. Also: cite the visual checklist by name, not line number (35 citations today; it has thirteen lines and `ARCHITECTURE.md` says twelve); fold answered open questions into their chapters; move dated history into the records.

### D4. Two taste calls, both yours
- **`36%` beside or instead of `.36`.** `.081` against `.81` is a tenfold misread at 11 px, and the same screen prints both. About a session and a half with the formatter moved to the browser first; your two-figure rule and its guards do not change either way. *No recommendation — taste.*
- **Routes, seed and loop counts move off the always-on strip into a *Run details* section of the panel** (never a dialog). Both reviews asked independently; nothing is lost, it is one click away. *Recommended.*

---

## What the coordinator decided without asking, and how to overturn each

| The path-product item on `feat/04b-evals` was put on hold, then dropped; it was never started | Three analysts call it invalid (A3) | Say so; it is about one session to build |

1	# Red team — `design-after-midpoint-review.md` and `PLAN.md`
2	
3	**2026-09-21 · one read-only Opus analyst · no file in the repository or any worktree was
4	changed.** Scripts at
5	`/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/b70a1857-a894-4bbe-b3a6-4d7cf3ebc4f8/scratchpad/digest/redteam/`
6	(`rt_core.py`, `attack1.py`…`attack4.py`). I ran no paid call, no server, no whole suite, no
7	playwright. **PROVED** means I ran it or read it; **SUSPECT** means I argued it and did not
8	measure it. Every number below is mine unless I say otherwise.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## 1. Verdict
13	
14	**Sound with changes — but three of them are load-bearing and one is a straight error of
15	fact.** The engine reformulation is the right idea, the hazard model is right, the collapse
16	from event *times* to event *truths* is a genuinely good trade, and `Suppose this is true` comes
17	out exact to four decimal places; I could not break that. What is not true is the word
18	**exact**: under `This happened` the design does exact arithmetic on a table built from the
19	wrong timing, and I measured **0.124** of error on a four-claim map — twenty-five times the
20	worst gap the design quotes, on the product's second verb. Separately, `sustain` does not
21	survive §2.2 — so the event/state split is **required**, not optional, and the decision put to
22	Kent as a free choice is not one; and the cost line ("3 sessions, net −350 lines") is scoped to
23	the one file where the work is cheapest and omits `diff.py`, the browser, 60 tests and ~400
24	lines of spec.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## 2. Must change before Kent sees it
29	
30	### M1. "Solved exactly" is false under *This happened*. The design must say so and state a tolerance. — **PROVED**
31	
32	The design (§2.2): *"Whether each claim happens is then solved exactly … `This happened`
33	multiplies in the evidence and renormalises. Both exact."* The arithmetic is exact. **The table
34	it is applied to is not**, and an observation is exactly the operation that invalidates it.
35	
36	The forward pass produces each claim's arrival-time distribution **under the prior**. Evidence
37	moves a claim's arrival as well as its truth ("if B happened, A more likely happened early"),
38	and the design never rebuilds the tables. `do` is fine, because the design explicitly re-runs
39	the forward pass under it. `observe` is not.
40	
41	I wrote a faithful implementation of §2.2 (`rt_core.py`) and an exact-over-times reference,
42	with **all three arrow shapes** — the analyst's scripts use `step` only; the string `shape`
43	never appears in `ve_cost.py`, `pin_error.py` or `pin_error_many.py`, so the quoted .0065 and
44	.049 have never met an `impulse`, the one shape where timing is everything.
45	
46	Worst |design − exact| by map family (`attack1.py`, K = 24):
47	
48	| map | worst gap | where |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| the analyst's own map, my code (control) | .0022 | — |
51	| impulse, short half-life, near a deadline | .0001 | *(the design is fine here — see below)* |
52	| diamond, equal lags | .0055 | observe |
53	| chain, depth 6 / depth 10 | .0090 / .0109 | observe |
54	| diamond, lags 2 vs 34 | .0125 | observe |
55	| **strong inhibitor** | **.0229** | observe |
56	| **lag 26 days against a 28-day gap** | **.0338** | observe |
57	| **"race against the clock" chain, lag 9 of a 12-day gap** | **.0352** | observe |
58	
59	**Every gap over .01 is an observation.** Over 140 adversarially generated four-claim maps
60	(`attack2.py` §B, tight deadlines, lags up to 70 % of each gap, mixed shapes — 9 520 compared
61	numbers):
62	
63	| query | n | mean | p99 | worst | **share off by more than .005** |
64	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
65	| no edit | 560 | .00027 | .0046 | .0175 | 0.9 % |
66	| `do` (Suppose) | 4 480 | .00007 | .0015 | .0259 | **0.2 %** |
67	| `observe` (This happened) | 4 480 | .00127 | .0151 | **.2043** | **6.6 %** |
68	
69	The worst case re-run at a finer grid is **not** a grid artefact: at K = 40 it is **.1242**
70	(exact .6318, design .5076), stable. Its shape: three parents, impulse arrows with long lags,
71	and an observation on a claim that is *also* a parent of another parent — so the evidence
72	shifts the second parent's arrival and the table never learns. In-degree 3 is what generation
73	is built to produce; 3 of the 19 arrows in the committed recording are `impulse`.
74	
75	**The mechanism, stated so it can be checked:** the error needs the evidence to move a
76	*parent's arrival time*. A plain chain A→R→M observed at R is exact to four places
77	(`attack3.py` §A) because "R happened" gives back exactly R's prior arrival conditional on
78	happening. It is when the evidence reaches a claim through two routes that the cut
79	approximation bites.
80	
81	**There is no cheap patch.** I tried the obvious one — rebuild the tables from the arrival
82	distributions the exact model has *after* conditioning, then redo the same truth solve. It
83	double-counts the evidence and makes the gap **worse**: on the lag-26 map, +.0338 becomes
84	+.0581; on the race chain, +.0352 becomes +.0501 (`attack2.py` §C).
85	
86	**Concrete edit.** In §2.2, replace *"Both exact"* with: *"`Suppose` is exact. `This happened`
87	is exact arithmetic on a table built from the prior's timing; measured against exact-over-times
88	it is within .005 on most maps and can reach .12 when the evidence reaches a claim by two
89	routes through impulse arrows."* Then pick one and write it down: (a) accept it and set the
90	displayed tolerance accordingly, or (b) rebuild the forward pass under evidence by iterating to
91	a fixed point, and cost it. Do not ship a screen that says two significant figures next to an
92	engine whose second figure moves.
93	
94	### M2. PLAN 05-1's oracle cannot catch a wrong table. Here is the test that can. — **PROVED by construction**
95	
96	PLAN 05-1: *"a brute-force enumerator over ≤5-claim maps asserting every number to 1e-9 against
97	the exact core."* At `1e-9` there are only two possibilities, and both are bad: either the
98	enumerator builds the same yes/no tables the core does — in which case it proves the variable
99	elimination is right and is **blind to everything in M1** — or it builds them independently,
100	in which case it cannot pass at `1e-9` at all and the tolerance gets loosened until it does.
101	Either way the timing approximation is invisible, and the project's headline test would be
102	certifying the one thing that is wrong.
103	
104	**Write two tests, with two tolerances, proving two different things.**
105	
106	1. **`test_the_elimination_is_exact`** — tolerance `1e-9`. The enumerator takes **the core's own
107	   yes/no tables** and sums the 2ⁿ joint by hand, applying `do` as a point mass and `observe` as
108	   a mask-and-renormalise. This proves the elimination, the `do` surgery and the conditioning.
109	   Cheap, fast, and it is what 05-1 actually describes.
110	2. **`test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time`** — tolerance **measured, not aspirational**.
111	   The enumerator is forbidden the core's tables and is built **from the arrow parameters alone**
112	   (`q0`, `q1`, `lag`, `shape`, `half_life`, the deadline): it enumerates the full
113	   `(K+1)ⁿ` first-passage joint at a fine grid for n ≤ 4, conditions there, and reports
114	   `1 − P(never)`. This is the only test that can see M1. It must run `do` **and** `observe`,
115	   and it must include an impulse arrow and a diamond, because a step-shaped chain does not
116	   reproduce the defect. `rt_core.exact_over_times` is a working 80-line version of this
117	   enumerator; it is in the scratchpad and can be lifted.
118	
119	Set test 2's tolerance from a measured sweep and **write the number in the record**, so that if
120	someone later tightens the model the test tells them.
121	
122	### M3. `sustain` does not survive §2.2. The event/state split is required, and the decision Kent is being offered is not a real choice. — **PROVED**
123	
124	Today (`propagation.py:1431-1434`) a `sustain` arrow pushes with `truth[source]` — the source's
125	truth **read on every day** — and a `trigger` arrow with `fired[source]`, one flag per world.
126	They differ only because today a claim can **un-resolve** when an impulse fades
127	(`propagation.py:1444`) — which is defect E5, the thing §2.2 removes on purpose.
128	
129	Under first passage `truth[source]` on day *t* is exactly `1 if τ_source ≤ t`, which is
130	monotone and absorbing. So a `sustain` arrow pushes from `τ_source + lag` onward — and so does
131	a `trigger` arrow with the same `shape` and `lag`. I built both: identical to six decimal
132	places (`attack3.py` §B). **`mode` becomes dead data, fully determined by `shape`.** And the
133	one mechanism that can un-true a claim today — automatic retraction — is precisely what record
134	0017 deletes. ADR-0005 calls `trigger`/`sustain` *"the best idea in the brainstorm"*
135	(`docs/adr/0005:72`).
136	
137	So §2.3's framing — *"offered to Kent as OPTIONAL … the engine does not depend on it"* — is
138	wrong in the way that matters. §2.2 does not merely leave `sustain` unimproved; it **deletes**
139	it. The design's own parenthetical half-sees this (*"this split may be required by §2.2, not
140	optional"*) and then the sentence beside it says the engine lands either way. Both cannot be true.
141	
142	**And a state is not one yes/no variable.** A state holds over an interval; its children read
143	the hazard integrated over that interval. Four maps in which "did it ever hold?" is YES in every
144	row, differing only in when the state switched on and off, give the child **.148, .193, .215,
145	.827** (`attack3.py` §C) — 0.68 of probability spread across maps a single bit cannot tell
146	apart. A state claim in the binary network therefore needs **two** times, on and off, and its
147	"truth" variable has to be *defined* ("holds at the deadline"? "ever held"? they are different
148	questions and the tile sentence must say which).
149	
150	**Concrete edits.** (i) In §2.3, move event/state out of "three things that ride with it" and
151	into §2.2 as a consequence, with the honest sentence: *"`mode` no longer does anything on its
152	own. Either claims split into events and states, or `sustain` is deleted from the vocabulary and
153	`shape` carries the whole distinction."* (ii) Say what a state claim's number means, in one
154	sentence, before any code. (iii) Offer Kent the cheap third option nobody has written down:
155	**keep events only and express a sustained push as two arrows** — one from the onset event and
156	an inhibitor from the ending event. That reproduces `sustain` exactly under first passage, costs
157	a validity rule and a prompt sentence instead of a wire field and a schema change, and it is the
158	option that does *not* move the fingerprint twice. (iv) Re-cost: the engine digest prices
159	event/state at 1.3 sessions *on top of* §2.2's three, and §2.2's "3 sessions" does not include it.
160	
161	### M4. `series` cannot keep its meaning, and the design says it does. — **PROVED**
162	
163	§2.2's "Kept untouched" list includes *"the `World` and `Diff` shapes the browser reads"*, and
164	the engine digest spells out that `series` *"keeps its type and its meaning"*. It cannot.
165	
166	Today `series` is an **instantaneous** per-day likelihood that is explicitly allowed to fall.
167	`tests/unit/fixtures/test_hormuz_golden.py:117-120` pins it:
168	
169	```
170	assert strike.series["H"][0] == 1.0
171	assert 0.25 < strike.series["H"][1] < 0.45
172	assert strike.series["H"][1] == strike.series["H"][3]
173	assert strike.series["H"][4] < 0.10
174	```
175	
176	`1.0 → .36 → .36 → <.10`. Under *"the chance it happens by day t"* the series is a cumulative
177	curve: **monotone non-decreasing, never falling.** `1.0 → .36` is arithmetically impossible.
178	`test_hormuz_golden.py:81` also pins `series["B"][1] < series["B"][2]` after a fall. This is the
179	largest unadmitted change in the proposal and it is hiding inside the field the design was most
180	confident about. It takes `DeltaRow.peak_delta` and `at_day` with it — their whole rationale
181	("shows up for a fortnight and then unwinds") presumes a curve that can unwind.
182	
183	**It also answers the red-team question about a dated observation.** Under *This happened on
184	day 5* the coherent per-day object is `P(τ ≤ t | evidence)` — which the design **can** state,
185	but only if the yes/no variable is re-cut per day, and that is a different (and larger) object
186	than the single "by its deadline" variable §2.2 describes. The design says *"every displayed day
187	rides along as an array axis"* and never says what the axis holds. **Decide this before the
188	first line of code**, and note the related contradiction: §2.2 says the forward pass runs at
189	*"12–24 points"*, the engine digest says *"~180 displayed days"* ride as elimination axes
190	(`propagation.py:110`, `SERIES_CAP = 180`). Those are different engines with different costs.
191	
192	### M5. "3 sessions, net −350 lines" is scoped to the easiest file. Five to seven is the floor. — **PROVED**
193

# Red team — `design-after-midpoint-review.md` and `PLAN.md`

**2026-09-21 · one read-only Opus analyst · no file in the repository or any worktree was
changed.** Scripts at
`/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/b70a1857-a894-4bbe-b3a6-4d7cf3ebc4f8/scratchpad/digest/redteam/`
(`rt_core.py`, `attack1.py`…`attack4.py`). I ran no paid call, no server, no whole suite, no
playwright. **PROVED** means I ran it or read it; **SUSPECT** means I argued it and did not
measure it. Every number below is mine unless I say otherwise.

---

## 1. Verdict

**Sound with changes — but three of them are load-bearing and one is a straight error of
fact.** The engine reformulation is the right idea, the hazard model is right, the collapse
from event *times* to event *truths* is a genuinely good trade, and `Suppose this is true` comes
out exact to four decimal places; I could not break that. What is not true is the word
**exact**: under `This happened` the design does exact arithmetic on a table built from the
wrong timing, and I measured **0.124** of error on a four-claim map — twenty-five times the
worst gap the design quotes, on the product's second verb. Separately, `sustain` does not
survive §2.2 — so the event/state split is **required**, not optional, and the decision put to
Kent as a free choice is not one; and the cost line ("3 sessions, net −350 lines") is scoped to
the one file where the work is cheapest and omits `diff.py`, the browser, 60 tests and ~400
lines of spec.

---

## 2. Must change before Kent sees it

### M1. "Solved exactly" is false under *This happened*. The design must say so and state a tolerance. — **PROVED**

The design (§2.2): *"Whether each claim happens is then solved exactly … `This happened`
multiplies in the evidence and renormalises. Both exact."* The arithmetic is exact. **The table
it is applied to is not**, and an observation is exactly the operation that invalidates it.

The forward pass produces each claim's arrival-time distribution **under the prior**. Evidence
moves a claim's arrival as well as its truth ("if B happened, A more likely happened early"),
and the design never rebuilds the tables. `do` is fine, because the design explicitly re-runs
the forward pass under it. `observe` is not.

I wrote a faithful implementation of §2.2 (`rt_core.py`) and an exact-over-times reference,
with **all three arrow shapes** — the analyst's scripts use `step` only; the string `shape`
never appears in `ve_cost.py`, `pin_error.py` or `pin_error_many.py`, so the quoted .0065 and
.049 have never met an `impulse`, the one shape where timing is everything.

Worst |design − exact| by map family (`attack1.py`, K = 24):

| map | worst gap | where |
|---|---|---|
| the analyst's own map, my code (control) | .0022 | — |
| impulse, short half-life, near a deadline | .0001 | *(the design is fine here — see below)* |
| diamond, equal lags | .0055 | observe |
| chain, depth 6 / depth 10 | .0090 / .0109 | observe |
| diamond, lags 2 vs 34 | .0125 | observe |
| **strong inhibitor** | **.0229** | observe |
| **lag 26 days against a 28-day gap** | **.0338** | observe |
| **"race against the clock" chain, lag 9 of a 12-day gap** | **.0352** | observe |

**Every gap over .01 is an observation.** Over 140 adversarially generated four-claim maps
(`attack2.py` §B, tight deadlines, lags up to 70 % of each gap, mixed shapes — 9 520 compared
numbers):

| query | n | mean | p99 | worst | **share off by more than .005** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no edit | 560 | .00027 | .0046 | .0175 | 0.9 % |
| `do` (Suppose) | 4 480 | .00007 | .0015 | .0259 | **0.2 %** |
| `observe` (This happened) | 4 480 | .00127 | .0151 | **.2043** | **6.6 %** |

The worst case re-run at a finer grid is **not** a grid artefact: at K = 40 it is **.1242**
(exact .6318, design .5076), stable. Its shape: three parents, impulse arrows with long lags,
and an observation on a claim that is *also* a parent of another parent — so the evidence
shifts the second parent's arrival and the table never learns. In-degree 3 is what generation
is built to produce; 3 of the 19 arrows in the committed recording are `impulse`.

**The mechanism, stated so it can be checked:** the error needs the evidence to move a
*parent's arrival time*. A plain chain A→R→M observed at R is exact to four places
(`attack3.py` §A) because "R happened" gives back exactly R's prior arrival conditional on
happening. It is when the evidence reaches a claim through two routes that the cut
approximation bites.

**There is no cheap patch.** I tried the obvious one — rebuild the tables from the arrival
distributions the exact model has *after* conditioning, then redo the same truth solve. It

### M2. PLAN 05-1's oracle cannot catch a wrong table. Here is the test that can. — **PROVED by construction**

PLAN 05-1: *"a brute-force enumerator over ≤5-claim maps asserting every number to 1e-9 against
the exact core."* At `1e-9` there are only two possibilities, and both are bad: either the
enumerator builds the same yes/no tables the core does — in which case it proves the variable
elimination is right and is **blind to everything in M1** — or it builds them independently,
in which case it cannot pass at `1e-9` at all and the tolerance gets loosened until it does.
Either way the timing approximation is invisible, and the project's headline test would be
certifying the one thing that is wrong.

**Write two tests, with two tolerances, proving two different things.**

1. **`test_the_elimination_is_exact`** — tolerance `1e-9`. The enumerator takes **the core's own
   yes/no tables** and sums the 2ⁿ joint by hand, applying `do` as a point mass and `observe` as
   a mask-and-renormalise. This proves the elimination, the `do` surgery and the conditioning.
   Cheap, fast, and it is what 05-1 actually describes.
2. **`test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time`** — tolerance **measured, not aspirational**.
   The enumerator is forbidden the core's tables and is built **from the arrow parameters alone**
   (`q0`, `q1`, `lag`, `shape`, `half_life`, the deadline): it enumerates the full
   `(K+1)ⁿ` first-passage joint at a fine grid for n ≤ 4, conditions there, and reports
   `1 − P(never)`. This is the only test that can see M1. It must run `do` **and** `observe`,
   and it must include an impulse arrow and a diamond, because a step-shaped chain does not
   reproduce the defect. `rt_core.exact_over_times` is a working 80-line version of this
   enumerator; it is in the scratchpad and can be lifted.

Set test 2's tolerance from a measured sweep and **write the number in the record**, so that if
someone later tightens the model the test tells them.

### M3. `sustain` does not survive §2.2. The event/state split is required, and the decision Kent is being offered is not a real choice. — **PROVED**

Today (`propagation.py:1431-1434`) a `sustain` arrow pushes with `truth[source]` — the source's
truth **read on every day** — and a `trigger` arrow with `fired[source]`, one flag per world.
They differ only because today a claim can **un-resolve** when an impulse fades
(`propagation.py:1444`) — which is defect E5, the thing §2.2 removes on purpose.

Under first passage `truth[source]` on day *t* is exactly `1 if τ_source ≤ t`, which is
monotone and absorbing. So a `sustain` arrow pushes from `τ_source + lag` onward — and so does
a `trigger` arrow with the same `shape` and `lag`. I built both: identical to six decimal
places (`attack3.py` §B). **`mode` becomes dead data, fully determined by `shape`.** And the
one mechanism that can un-true a claim today — automatic retraction — is precisely what record
0017 deletes. ADR-0005 calls `trigger`/`sustain` *"the best idea in the brainstorm"*
(`docs/adr/0005:72`).

So §2.3's framing — *"offered to Kent as OPTIONAL … the engine does not depend on it"* — is
wrong in the way that matters. §2.2 does not merely leave `sustain` unimproved; it **deletes**
it. The design's own parenthetical half-sees this (*"this split may be required by §2.2, not
optional"*) and then the sentence beside it says the engine lands either way. Both cannot be true.

**And a state is not one yes/no variable.** A state holds over an interval; its children read
the hazard integrated over that interval. Four maps in which "did it ever hold?" is YES in every
row, differing only in when the state switched on and off, give the child **.148, .193, .215,
.827** (`attack3.py` §C) — 0.68 of probability spread across maps a single bit cannot tell
apart. A state claim in the binary network therefore needs **two** times, on and off, and its
"truth" variable has to be *defined* ("holds at the deadline"? "ever held"? they are different
questions and the tile sentence must say which).

**Concrete edits.** (i) In §2.3, move event/state out of "three things that ride with it" and
into §2.2 as a consequence, with the honest sentence: *"`mode` no longer does anything on its
own. Either claims split into events and states, or `sustain` is deleted from the vocabulary and
`shape` carries the whole distinction."* (ii) Say what a state claim's number means, in one
sentence, before any code. (iii) Offer Kent the cheap third option nobody has written down:
**keep events only and express a sustained push as two arrows** — one from the onset event and
an inhibitor from the ending event. That reproduces `sustain` exactly under first passage, costs
a validity rule and a prompt sentence instead of a wire field and a schema change, and it is the
option that does *not* move the fingerprint twice. (iv) Re-cost: the engine digest prices
event/state at 1.3 sessions *on top of* §2.2's three, and §2.2's "3 sessions" does not include it.

### M7. The `q₀`/`q₁` wording is not a specification, and the interim derivation is wrong for `impulse` arrows. — **PROVED**

Design §4 elicits `p_effect_if_cause` / `p_effect_if_not_cause` with two comments. For a claim
with three causes they are ambiguous three ways: (a) what the *other* causes are doing is
unstated — "if the cause happens" invites a marginalised conditional, which is not what either
engine's calibration takes; (b) `q₀` is elicited once **per arrow**, so three arrows into one
claim yield three numbers that must all be equal, and a fourth (the claim's `prior`) that must
equal them too, with nothing enforcing it; (c) *when* the cause happens is unstated.

The only reading both engines can consume: **`q₀` = P(effect by its own deadline | none of the
causes on this map happens)** — a property of the *claim*, not the arrow, and identical to its
`prior`; **`q₁` = P(effect by that same deadline | this cause happens on the first day of the
window and no other cause on the map happens)**.

And the interim derivation does not hold. With `strength = logit(q₁) − logit(q₀)` on today's
engine, measured: `step` lag 0 → .7000 ✓, `step` lag 30 → .7000 ✓, `ramp` → .7000 ✓,
**`impulse` lag 7 half-life 14 → .2000 ✗** (the elicited `q₁` of .70 is discarded entirely; the
spike has faded by the day the claim is read). **3 of 19 arrows in the committed recording are
`impulse`.** So the same two elicited numbers mean measurably different things before and after
05-4 — which is a second reason to pin the window in the prompt, not the shape.

Also: the "free coherence check" (`p_child ≈ p_parent·q₁ + (1−p_parent)·q₀`) contradicts
"our code sets the leak to `q₀`". If `p_child` is the leak the residual is `p_parent·(q₁−q₀)`,
nonzero by construction on every arrow that does anything. 05-2 freezes neither reading and
never mentions `prior`.

50	### 2.1 The rule that makes the comparison honest
51	
52	> **A model number may be differenced against a market quote only when both range over the same set of worlds — so the edge is computed from the world with *no supposition in force*, and a supposed world can only ever show a conditional payoff.**
53	
54	The smallest shape that enforces it is a **signature, not a guard**. The edge is never computed from "a world"; it is computed by one function that requires the base world as its own argument:
55	
56	```python
57	# katalyst/thesis/edge.py — outside domain/, because it touches a quote (INV-11, ADR-0003)
58	
59	class Quote(BaseModel):                     # what a venue says. Never merged with a model number.
60	    venue: str; contract_id: str
61	    p: float                                # the mid, as a probability
62	    spread: float                           # best offer minus best bid
63	    as_of: date; url: str
64	    source: Literal["fetched", "recorded", "user"]
65	
66	class Edge(BaseModel):                      # built by `priced()` and nowhere else
67	    model: Belief                           # unconditional, owner='model'
68	    quote: Quote
69	    costs: float                            # half the spread plus fees, as a probability
70	    edge: float                             # model.p − quote.p − costs. Signed. May be negative.
71	    break_even: float                       # quote.p + costs — useful even with no quote
72	    mixture: tuple[MixtureTerm, ...]        # every term shown: P(H)·P(c|do H) + (1−P(H))·P(c|do ¬H)
73	
74	class NotComparable(BaseModel):
75	    reason: Literal["conditional_world", "no_quote", "no_contract", "different_question"]
76	    said: str                               # the plain sentence the card prints
77	    break_even: float | None                # still printable when only the quote is missing
78	
79	def priced(base: World, shown: World, claim: PropositionId, quote: Quote | None) -> Edge | NotComparable: ...
80	```
81	
82	`base` and `shown` are two required arguments; there is no way to hand `priced` a branch world alone, and `Edge` has no other construction path. Tests: *agree with the market ⇒ edge reads exactly 0*; *a branch world alone does not type-check*; *a missing quote yields `NotComparable` that still prints the break-even.*

84	The **mixture** is the piece both reviews wanted and neither costed: after *Suppose Hormuz opens*, the card still says *"your supposition makes M1 .61; weighted by the map's own P(H) = .36 against the no-open world's .40, the unconditional number is .47 — that is the one compared with .48."* review/'s worked example, with the engine supplying the terms. 288	- **Recommended: amend INV-14 and FR-23 to say *watchlist*, and let the user own the stop.** Cost: ~0 lines of code; an ADR and three document edits. Buys: the one claim in the product a risk quant would call indefensible, removed.
289	- Alternative: keep the wording. Cost: nothing to build and a question nobody can answer in the demo.

295	- **I made no network call.** I do not know whether a Polymarket contract matching M1 exists today — hence D3. The recorded-quote design is deliberately robust to it not existing, but the demo's headline is not.
296	- **I did not run the frontend, Playwright, `make eval`, or anything that calls a model or costs money**, per the common brief.
297	- **I did not re-run the strike-branch numbers myself** (`apply` is not exported from `domain/branch.py` under that name and I stopped rather than hunt). I relied on `spec/multiverse/propagation.md:456`, which records the engine's own `.46 → .41` and `.43 → .36`.
298	- **I did not measure** how long a 20 000-draw daily path simulation takes over the Hormuz map. I estimate milliseconds in numpy over a `(20000, 45)` float array, but I did not run it. If it is slow, the draw count is the knob.
299	- **I did not verify** that the engine's `truth` array is still shaped `(versions, worlds, days)` end-to-end under every branch — I read `propagation.py:1444-1463` and confirmed the assignment, not the full lifetime.
300	- **I did not read** audit-G (generation) or audit-H (UX) in full, only their finance-adjacent rows; ENGINE, GENERATION and UX analysts cover those.
301	- **I did not price** the browser work beyond a line estimate; audit-H's dock placement is assumed correct without my checking the Inspector's section stack myself.
302	- **Calibration is untested and stays untested.** Nothing in this design validates that the model's probabilities are any good. The card says so; that is all it can honestly do.

## 2. The design I recommend

### 2.1 The rule that makes the comparison honest

> **A model number may be differenced against a market quote only when both range over the same set of worlds — so the edge is computed from the world with *no supposition in force*, and a supposed world can only ever show a conditional payoff.**

The smallest shape that enforces it is a **signature, not a guard**. The edge is never computed from "a world"; it is computed by one function that requires the base world as its own argument:

```python
# katalyst/thesis/edge.py — outside domain/, because it touches a quote (INV-11, ADR-0003)

class Quote(BaseModel):                     # what a venue says. Never merged with a model number.
    venue: str; contract_id: str
    p: float                                # the mid, as a probability
    spread: float                           # best offer minus best bid
    as_of: date; url: str
    source: Literal["fetched", "recorded", "user"]

class Edge(BaseModel):                      # built by `priced()` and nowhere else
    model: Belief                           # unconditional, owner='model'
    quote: Quote
    costs: float                            # half the spread plus fees, as a probability
    edge: float                             # model.p − quote.p − costs. Signed. May be negative.
    break_even: float                       # quote.p + costs — useful even with no quote
    mixture: tuple[MixtureTerm, ...]        # every term shown: P(H)·P(c|do H) + (1−P(H))·P(c|do ¬H)

class NotComparable(BaseModel):
    reason: Literal["conditional_world", "no_quote", "no_contract", "different_question"]
    said: str                               # the plain sentence the card prints
    break_even: float | None                # still printable when only the quote is missing

def priced(base: World, shown: World, claim: PropositionId, quote: Quote | None) -> Edge | NotComparable: ...
```

`base` and `shown` are two required arguments; there is no way to hand `priced` a branch world alone, and `Edge` has no other construction path. Tests: *agree with the market ⇒ edge reads exactly 0*; *a branch world alone does not type-check*; *a missing quote yields `NotComparable` that still prints the break-even.*

The **mixture** is the piece both reviews wanted and neither costed: after *Suppose Hormuz opens*, the card still says *"your supposition makes M1 .61; weighted by the map's own P(H) = .36 against the no-open world's .40, the unconditional number is .47 — that is the one compared with .48."* review/'s worked example, with the engine supplying the terms. It needs only `do(¬A)`, which exists.

### 2.2 What a stop-loss honestly is here

Four things, kept apart on the card, three of them named differently from today:

| Card section | What it is | Who owns it | How it is computed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What takes you out** | The events over-represented in the worlds where the stop was touched **first** | computed | `lift(k) = P(k happened before the stop ∣ stop first) / P(k happened)`, Wilson interval on the numerator, suppressed below 200 draws, with the median days between *k* and the stop |
| **What to watch** | The claim whose adverse flip hurts the terminal most, **and** resolves before it, **and** is publicly observable | computed | two-directional `sensitivity()` + INV-14's two filters. *Renamed from "invalidation"; it is a watchlist, not a stop.* |
| **Your risk exit** | The stop price, the target, the horizon | **the user types them** | never derived |
| **Execution** | — | — | We say one sentence: *a stop order's trigger is not its fill price*, and nothing else. |

**The smallest thing that is both honest and impressive is "what takes you out".** Forty lines over a boolean mask; the brief's most distinctive sentence answered by computation rather than prose; the one output nobody in the competitive landscape ships. "What to watch" is fifteen lines and is the honest remnant of INV-14. Everything above them — expected shortfall, ruin, drawdown — is cut.

**What each needs from the engine.** Only one thing, and it is small:

```python
# katalyst/thesis/draws.py — the ONLY coupling between the finance layer and the engine
class Draws(BaseModel):
    day_zero: date; days: int
    order: tuple[PropositionId, ...]
    when:   NDArray[int]      # (n, claims): the day each claim first became true, −1 for never
    weight: NDArray[float]    # (n,): all ones for an exact ancestral sampler
```

"What to watch" needs **endpoint marginals only** — today's `sensitivity()` gives them. P(stop first) / P(target first) need **event times per world**. The inverse query needs **joint samples with times**. All three come from `when`.

`weight` is in the shape from day one so the finance layer is **indifferent to ENGINE's Plan A versus Plan B**: an exact core with an ancestral sampler gives weights of one, a likelihood-weighted sampler gives real weights, and nothing above changes. And `when` is derivable from *today's* engine too — `_draw` already computes `truth[claim] = came_true`, a `(versions, worlds, days)` boolean array, whose first true day **is** `when`. **So stack 05 is not blocked on the engine reformulation**: write it against synthetic `Draws`, test it against synthetic `Draws`, turn it on over whichever engine lands.

| **Market data** | FRED is an observation, not a belief; recorded snapshots until live adapters exist | Polymarket keyless mid; user-entered first, ship in 05 | **Both, combined.** review/ is right about FRED; review2 is right that the user-entered path ships first and is forty lines. |
| **What "priced in" costs** | A design risk to fix before implementation | A blocker with ~60 lines of fix | **review2 on the size, review/ on the urgency.** It is cheap *and* it must be settled before the first line of 05. |

Where they **agree**, and both are right: the conditional-versus-unconditional trap (independently found, which is the strongest signal in either document); invalidation ≠ stop-loss; path products must go; the fixture's numbers contradict its prose; there is no position for a shock to hurt; and a conditional thesis with an honest *"no positive edge at this price"* is a complete result, not a failure.

---

## 4. What changes for the branches in flight

| Branch | Verdict | What changes, concretely |
|---|---|---|
| `fix/04-vanishing-wire` | **Keep, land first.** | Nothing from me. It may explain the growth branch's two unexplained cold-run failures. |
| `feat/04a-growth` | **Keep.** | Nothing from me. Its `frontend/src/world/absence.ts` correctly assumes the `market` slot is always absent today; stack 05's PR 4 is what fills it. |
| `fix/04-payoff-kind-required` | **Rescope — this is the decision gate for stack 05.** | It moves the prompt fingerprint (`1c224cc3…` → `ed0763b5…`), so `backend/recordings/hormuz.jsonl` must be re-recorded (~$4, ~36 min). | `feat/04b-recordings` | **Reorder — hold all three remaining recordings.** | RESUME already says to hold them for item 6; I am confirming it with a reason from stack 05, and adding one more condition: hold until D1 is answered. Re-recording Hormuz is unavoidable; re-recording it *twice* is not. |

Moving it into `domain/` blesses it permanently. Replace the **verdict** with total effect `P(B∣do A) − P(B∣do ¬A)` — which stack 05's mixture needs anyway, so it is written once and pays twice — and replace the **honesty bar** (FR-11's purpose, the conjunction fallacy) with a base-rate anchor on the headline.
